etymologies.etymologyHTML: From bore +‎ -dom.

quote.citation: 1852 March – 1853 September, Charles Dickens, chapter XII, in Bleak House, London: Bradbury and Evans, […], published 1853, →OCLC:
quote.text: […] only last Sunday, my Lady, in the desolation of Boredom and the clutch of Giant Despair, almost hated her own maid for being in spirits.

definitions.definition: (countable) An instance or period of being bored; A bored state.

quote.citation: 1995, Martin Heidegger, William McNeill, Nicholas Walker, transl., The Fundamental Concepts of Metaphysics: World, Finitude, Solitude, page 107:
quote.text: If we are seeking a more original conception of boredom then we must also correspondingly endeavour to envisage a more original form of boredom, thus presumably a boredom in which we become more bored than in the situation we have characterized.

quote.citation: 1999, Michael L. Raposa, Boredom and the Religious Imagination‎[1], page 58:
quote.text: Yet that earlier characterization was of a kind of boredom that can be portrayed as resembling acedia; that is, a boredom that I can be held responsible for, either in its genesis or its persistence.
